strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: improving instruction tuning without additional data curation. The recipe is understandable, combining confidence-based pairing and hidden-state Mixup with the standard next-token prediction objective.

The empirical coverage is substantial. Table 1 reports consistent improvements across seven model–dataset configurations, with MT-Bench overall gains of approximately 0.20–0.40. Medical QA results provide complementary evidence, improving average accuracy by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral, respectively.

Human evaluation provides useful corroboration: SFTMix receives 42.5% wins versus 26.5% for NTP across 200 judgments on 80 prompts. Experiments with LoRA, data selection, weaker reference models, and multilingual tuning also support the recipe’s applicability.
weaknesses: The central confidence-based design is insufficiently isolated. There is no direct comparison with ordinary random-pair Mixup under otherwise identical conditions. Section 5.2 changes the response distribution to compare high- and low-quality data, but omits confidence-based pairing on that same modified dataset. Consequently, it does not establish that training-dynamics confidence is crucial. This missing control is decisive because generic Mixup could explain the reported gains.

Evaluation reliability remains unresolved. Appendix A.1 selects hyperparameters using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, which also supply the headline results; no separate validation set is identified. Five evaluation rounds do not establish robustness across training seeds, and confidence intervals or significance tests are absent. This matters for relatively small improvements, including a 0.32-point increase in length-controlled win rate. The human study also omits annotator counts, assignment details, and agreement statistics. Transfer to other settings mitigates these concerns but does not fully resolve them.

The proposed mechanism exceeds the evidence. Separation in a t-SNE visualization and a 7% reduction in confidence-score standard deviation do not demonstrate reduced overfitting on confident examples or improved generalization on unconfident examples. Section 3.4 establishes that the auxiliary objective changes gradients, without establishing the claimed generalization effects. Evaluation of held-out performance and generalization gaps by confidence group would directly test this explanation.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the reported optimizer and training defaults. Important omissions include checkpoint timing for confidence estimation, maximum sequence lengths and truncation settings, LoRA configuration, and exact generation and judge configurations. No implementation link is provided. These details affect both the learned confidence partition and measured performance.

The distinction from the cited cartography-based Mixup work of Park and Caragea (2022) needs clearer treatment. Extending such ideas to autoregressive instruction tuning is potentially valuable, but the manuscript does not adequately distinguish its methodological contribution from this close precedent. This limits the main-conference case independently of soundness.

The practical cost is insufficiently characterized. SFTMix requires reference-model fine-tuning and checkpoint scoring in addition to target-model training, yet no end-to-end compute measurements or equal-budget comparison are reported. The weaker-reference experiment is encouraging but narrow. Overall, the consistent empirical gains make Findings plausible, while the missing central control and unresolved evaluation and reproducibility issues prevent a clear positive recommendation.
